# The Collectors

## I.

The milk was three days past its date, which by Vera's metric meant it had three days left. She poured it over the cereal and listened to it hit the bowl with a sound like a small question. She ate standing up. There hadn't been a clear chair since 2019, and the kitchen table was currently hosting a collection of takeout menus from restaurants that had closed during the pandemic, arranged alphabetically by cuisine, weighted down by a VCR she fully intended to repair once she found the right screwdriver, which was in one of the eleven toolboxes, which were in the hall closet behind the sewing machine and the three vacuum cleaners, two of which worked.

She had a system. She had paths. The apartment was navigable if you understood its grammar — turn sideways past the magazines, duck under the hanging rack of coats she'd bought at estate sales (the dead deserved to have their clothes appreciated, not landfilled), keep left where the newspapers fanned out from the bathroom door like a paper delta. She knew where everything was. She could find any object in under four minutes, which was better than most people could do in their empty, echoing homes, with their blank counters and bare walls and the constant quiet hum of all the things they'd thrown away.

The letter was on the counter between a stack of expired coupons and a bread machine still in its box. She'd read it three times. The first time standing, the second time sitting on the floor because her knees went, the third time with a kind of cold taxonomic focus, as though she could file its contents into a category that would make them manageable. The envelope was cream-colored, hand-addressed, no return address. The stamp was a forever stamp from 2016 — a detail that meant nothing and that she couldn't stop cataloging.

She put her cereal bowl in the sink, which is to say she placed it on top of the other bowls in the sink, a ceramic cairn marking the days. She picked up her phone. It was an old iPhone in a case she'd kept from two models ago because the new case didn't have the same texture against her palm, and she wasn't going to just *discard* something that still held the shape of her hand.

The number was in her contacts under a single initial. M. She hadn't called it in eleven years. She hadn't deleted it either, because you don't delete things — that was the whole point, that was the architecture of a life that understood that everything you let go of leaves a hole, and enough holes and you're nothing, you're air, you're the weight a dead boy stops having when no one alive will hold it.

She pressed call.

It rang four times. A woman answered with the clipped, guarded voice of someone who screens every call and had picked up this one by mistake.

"It's Vera," Vera said.

Silence. Then: "Jesus Christ."

"Did you get a letter?"

A longer silence. "I'm hanging up now."

"Margot. *Did you get a letter.*"

She could hear Margot breathing. She could hear, faintly, the ambient noise of an office — other voices, a printer, the civilized machinery of a life that worked.

"Yes," Margot said. "I got a letter."

---

## II.

Margot Kessler, attorney-at-law, had been in a partners' meeting when her fingers closed around David Chen's Montblanc. She didn't decide to take it. Her hand decided. Her hand had been deciding things like this for twenty-six years, ever since the summer she was twelve and learned that you could take something that didn't belong to you and the world would keep turning, and the secret of having it — the private, swallowed thrill of possession without permission — was the only thing that had ever made her feel like she had a say in what happened next.

She'd excused herself, gone to the bathroom, looked at the pen. Matte black, gold clip, probably four hundred dollars. She didn't want it. She didn't want any of it — not the hotel soaps she pocketed on work trips, not the paperweights she lifted from other people's desks, not the lighters she took from restaurant tables though she didn't smoke. She didn't want any of it. She just needed the *taking*.

The letter had been in her mailbox on Tuesday. She'd opened it at the island in her kitchen — granite, spotless, nothing on the counter but a single orchid she kept alive through punishing discipline. She read the letter once. She folded it, slid it back into the envelope, and put the envelope in her jacket pocket in one fluid motion, as though someone might see her with it, as though it was stolen property, which in a way it was — stolen time, stolen silence, two decades of a life she'd shoplifted from the world by never confessing what she'd done when she was twelve.

---

Neil Russo's wife, Janine, believed he had insomnia. This was technically true. What she didn't know was that the insomnia had a shape, and the shape was a poker interface glowing blue-white in the bathroom at 3 a.m., and beneath the interface was not the desire to win (he usually lost; the math worked against everyone eventually, and he understood the math, he'd been an actuary for nine years) but the desire to *not know what was about to happen* — the exquisite, annihilating instant between the bet and the reveal, when the future hadn't collapsed into fact yet, when anything was possible, when for one half-second the universe held its breath and so did he.

The letter was propped against his monitor. He'd read it and grinned. He couldn't help it. It was the same grin he'd felt when the bet went in and the cards were still facedown: here at last was something with *stakes*. Real ones. Not chips, not points, not the abstract numerics of risk management — actual stakes, the kind you couldn't calculate or hedge, the kind that could ruin your whole life in a single reveal. His pulse was up. His hands were steady. He felt, for the first time in months, awake.

---

Debra Holtz was making a bouillabaisse for the Abbotts when the letter arrived. She had been the Abbotts' private chef for six years. She fed their family of five, three meals a day, weekdays, with a meal plan she designed each Sunday that accounted for macronutrient balance, seasonal availability, and Mrs. Abbott's constantly shifting list of intolerances. She fed them beautifully. She fed them with precision. She fed everyone but herself with any coherence at all.

On Tuesdays and Thursdays, after service, she drove to the storage unit she rented off Route 9 and ate until the contents of her body felt like a wall. Then she emptied the wall. The she drove home, showered, slept, and arrived at the Abbotts' kitchen at 6 a.m. to do it again.

She read the letter while the bouillabaisse simmered. The paper shook in her hands. *I know what you buried behind Cabin 6. Be there Friday at sundown, all four, or I mail the proof to everyone you've built your life around.* She tore the letter in half. Then in quarters. Then she sat on the kitchen floor with a roll of Scotch tape and put it back together, piece by piece, until the words were whole again, a jigsaw of threat held together by adhesive, because destroying things and then reconstructing them was the motion her life was built around and she could no more leave a thing destroyed than she could leave herself unfed or fed or whatever the word was for what she did, which wasn't eating and wasn't not-eating but was something in between that took up all the room.

---

Four letters. Same cream envelope. Same hand-addressed block print. Same forever stamp from 2016.

Vera folded hers and filed it between utility bills in the kitchen stack, a piece of mail among mail, a threat absorbed into the collection.

Margot put hers in her pocket.

Debra taped hers back together.

Neil grinned.

---

## III.

The camp was two hours north of the nearest town that still had a gas station. The access road was unpaved, narrowing to a single lane where the pines closed in, and the gravel lot at the end of it hadn't been plowed or maintained in what looked like a decade. Weeds came up through the stones. A padlocked gate, chain-link, leaned at an angle that suggested it had been forced open and then re-secured more than once.

Vera arrived first. She parked her rental at the far end of the lot and spent eleven minutes in the car, inventorying: the gate, the tree line, the security camera she spotted on a post by the entrance (old, possibly functional, possibly not, she cataloged it either way), the smell of pine and standing water, the quality of the light through the canopy. She was building the room in her mind, filling it with data, because data was weight and weight was safety.

Margot arrived second, seven minutes after, in a black sedan she parked at the opposite end of the lot. She got out, saw Vera's car, and stood very still for a moment before walking over. She was wearing a gray blazer over a black turtleneck, the uniform of a woman who had been performing authority for so long it had almost become real.

"You look the same," Margot said.

"You don't," Vera said. Then, because she couldn't help it: "You still bite your left thumbnail down to the quick."

Margot put her hand in her pocket.

Debra came third, in a white compact that pulled in slowly, carefully, the car of someone accustomed to measuring every approach. She was thinner than she'd been at twelve, which was to say she was thin in a way that made Vera want to count her vertebrae through her shirt. She got out and stood by her car and didn't walk toward them and didn't walk away, just stood in the middle distance like someone waiting for permission to arrive.

"Debra," Vera called.

Debra crossed the lot. Up close her eyes were dark-ringed and her lips were chapped and she smelled, very faintly, of saffron and stomach acid.

"I haven't eaten since Tuesday," Debra said, to no one, to the air.

"That's—" Margot started.

"I'm not looking for commentary," Debra said. "I'm stating a fact about my body so we can move past it."

They stood in the gravel lot — three women in their early thirties who had last been in the same place when they were twelve and terrified and digging in the dark — and looked at each other with the blunt, appraising wariness of strangers who shared a single ungovernable memory.

Neil Russo was twenty minutes late. They heard him before they saw him — whistling, a low tuneless thread of sound that came up the access road ahead of his footsteps. He'd parked down the hill, apparently. He came through the tree line on foot, hands in his pockets, and he was smiling, and the smile was the same one Vera remembered from the summer they were twelve: not cruel, not warm, just *alert*, the smile of someone who was always calculating odds.

"Ladies," he said.

"Don't," said Margot.

"Twenty years," Neil said. He looked at each of them in turn, taking his time, like he was reading a hand. "Vera, you look like you haven't thrown anything away since the Clinton administration, and I mean that with genuine respect. Margot, the blazer's great, very network-television lawyer, I can see it. Debra—"

"Neil," Vera said.

"—you look like you need a sandwich, but I'm told that's not something we—"

"*Neil.*"

He stopped. He stood there in the gravel lot with his hands in his pockets and his twenty-years-older face and a stillness that might have been respect but was more likely calculation.

"So," he said. "Anyone want to talk about Marcus Pruitt?"

The name hit the air like a slap. Debra took a step back. Margot's hand came out of her pocket, thumbnail already at her teeth. Vera felt her body do its thing — the cataloging, the inventory, the immediate and total absorption of a new piece of data into the filing system of her nervous system. *Marcus Pruitt. Age eleven. Brown hair. Gap in his front teeth. Pittsburgh Steelers jersey, the one with the mustard stain on the sleeve. Buried thirty-seven inches deep in clay soil that smelled like iron. July 19th. Air temperature approximately—*

"You don't say his name," Margot said. Her voice was low and even and her thumbnail was bleeding. "We agreed. You don't say his name."

"We agreed when we were twelve," Neil said. "And I don't recall the agreement holding up particularly well, given that we're all here because someone—"

"You think this is funny?" Debra said.

"I think it's interesting."

"A dead child is *interesting* to you?"

"Everything's interesting to me. That's the whole problem." He said it without affectation, without self-pity, just a flat diagnostic statement. Then, to Vera: "You called Margot. Margot called you." He pointed at Debra. "Which means one of you called me. Which means you all decided to come. Which means you all have lives that can be ruined. Which means whoever sent those letters knew that." He paused. "The question is whether we're here to protect what we have or to finally stop protecting it."

"We're here because we don't have a choice," Margot said.

"Everyone has a choice. That's what makes it terrible."

Vera watched the group dynamics reassemble in real time, the old architecture emerging from the ruin: Margot taking charge because someone had to; Debra retreating into her body; Neil pushing because pushing was the only way he could feel the edge. And herself, standing slightly apart, recording everything, accruing detail the way she accrued objects — compulsively, protectively, as though enough information could insulate her from the thing the information was about.

"After that summer," Vera said quietly, "two of us wanted to go to the police."

"Me and Debra," said Margot.

"And two of us didn't," Neil said. "Me and Vera. Because Vera couldn't let go of the secret — couldn't let go of *anything* — and I couldn't walk away from a bet I was winning."

"You were *twelve*," Debra said.

"I was twelve and I already knew what I was," Neil said. "Didn't you?"

No one answered. The pines moved in the wind. Somewhere on the property, a speaker crackled, then went silent.

"We should go in," Vera said.

---

## IV.

The padlock gave way to a bolt cutter Vera had brought in her bag, along with two flashlights, a first aid kit, a bundle of zip ties, a Swiss Army knife, three granola bars, and a Ziploc of assorted batteries she'd been carrying in her purse for two years. Margot looked at the bag's contents and said nothing. Debra looked at the granola bars and looked away.

The path to Cabin 6 was overgrown but navigable, a tunnel through sumac and wild grape, the camp's old trail markers still visible on the trees — faded paint blazes, yellow on bark, pointing toward a place that no longer existed in any form they recognized. The bunks were gone or collapsed. The lake was a green-brown absence visible through the trees, its dock rotted to a row of posts. The infirmary was a shell. The mess hall still stood, its tin roof rusted to the color of dried blood.

Cabin 6 still stood too. Barely. One wall had buckled and the roof sagged and the front steps were gone, replaced by a cinder block someone had placed there recently — the concrete was clean, unstained.

They stood behind the cabin. The ground sloped gently toward the woods. There was a depression in the earth, roughly six feet long, covered in pine needles and bracken. It could have been anything — a drainage ditch, a root collapse, the remnant of some camp maintenance project long forgotten. It could have been anything, but it wasn't anything. It was where they'd put Marcus Pruitt when they were twelve years old.

No one spoke for a long time. The depression sat in the earth like a held breath.

"It was smaller," Debra said finally.

"You were smaller," Neil said.
